workLog.task: Verify that #3362 was superseded before reworking it
workLog.outcome: PR #3359 landed the atomic write on 2026-07-26 and closed #3357, the issue PR #3362 targeted, so #3362 was a competing implementation of a shipped fix. Diffed the two rather than assuming the merged one was complete. Main is ahead on the exit-code contract: it separates exit 3 (filesystem refused the write) from exit 1 (malformed input) per ADR-035, and preserves the primary error when close() itself fails. The branch was ahead on two things main lacks, so those became #3368 instead of a rewrite of #3362.
workLog.evidence: gh issue view 3357 reports CLOSED; gh pr view 3359 --json closingIssuesReferences returns 3357. git log on scripts/validation/merge_causal_graph.py shows 3d1f3b30d2 'write causal graph merges atomically (#3359)'.

workLog.task: Measure the temporary-file leak before fixing it
workLog.outcome: Confirmed the leak is real, not theoretical. Cleanup in _atomic_write_text is attached to except OSError. KeyboardInterrupt is not an OSError, and a merge driver runs inside an interactive git merge, which is exactly where Ctrl-C lands. The destination survives; the temporary does not get removed, and tempfile.mkstemp's default name carries no link to what wrote it, so a leaked file in .agents/memory/causality/ is unattributable and one git add -A from being committed.
workLog.evidence: Probe against origin/main at 3d1f3b30d2, forcing a BaseException out of the write: 'main leaks on BaseException: [tmpzh8km2lu.tmp]' with 'destination intact: {"a":1}'.

workLog.outcome: Added an except BaseException handler that discards the temporary and re-raises, so an interrupt cleans up. Added handle.flush() and os.fsync(handle.fileno()) before the chmod and rename, because os.replace is atomic against other processes but not against a crash: without the sync a power loss after the rename can leave the destination naming data that never reached disk, which is the partial-file outcome #3359 set out to prevent, relocated from the write to the rename. Gave mkstemp a prefix derived from the destination name so any leak is greppable. Extracted _discard() so both handlers share one unlink and neither replaces the primary error with a cleanup error.
workLog.evidence: 73 tests pass in tests/validation/test_merge_causal_graph.py. Three negative controls, each reverting one change: dropping the BaseException handler turns 2 red, dropping the fsync turns 2 red, dropping the mkstemp prefix turns 1 red; restoring returns 73 passed. ruff check and ruff format clean on both files.

workLog.action: Review found the BaseException cleanup unlinking the temporary without closing it. Correct: the two interrupt tests already written both unwind with the handle closed, so neither reached the case. On POSIX the unlink succeeds and leaks only a descriptor; on Windows an open file cannot be unlinked at all, so the cleanup added to stop the leak would itself leak. Added _release, which closes before discarding and returns a description of whichever step failed, and collapsed the five nested try blocks and three duplicated message builders in _atomic_write_text down to two try blocks and one. Dropped the untested 'failed to close temporary file descriptor' branch and replaced it with a suppressed os.close, since that path is only reachable while already unwinding. New test interrupts inside handle.write and asserts close ran, which is what makes it fail on Linux rather than only on Windows. Negative control removing the close from _release: 2 red, including the pre-existing close-failure test. Restored: 74 pass, up from 73.

Review found markdownLintRun claiming no markdown changed while the branch adds a .serena memory. True as stated and wrong. Ran the scoped lint: 0 files, because .markdownlint-cli2.yaml excludes .serena/**. Rewrote the evidence to say that, since an exclusion and a pass are not the same result.

workLog.task: Correct the fdopen ownership claim and cover the case it denied
workLog.outcome: The cleanup comment said 'fdopen never took ownership, so the raw descriptor is still ours', which is true for only one of the two ways io.open can fail. Measured on CPython: an invalid mode raises before it wraps the descriptor and leaves it open, while an unknown encoding raises after the FileIO exists and closes it on the way out. Because the handler catches BaseException, an interrupt can land on either side of that line. The behavior was already right, since the os.close sits inside contextlib.suppress(OSError), but the comment asserted the opposite of what the suppress exists for, so anyone tidying the code would have read the suppress as dead and deleted it. Rewrote the comment around the measurement and added the missing test for the branch it denied.
workLog.evidence: Probe: os.fdopen(fd, 'not-a-mode') raises ValueError and a following os.close(fd) succeeds; os.fdopen(fd, 'w', encoding='definitely-not-a-codec') raises LookupError and os.close(fd) answers EBADF. New test test_fdopen_that_closed_the_descriptor_before_failing_is_survivable patches fdopen to close then raise. Negative control removed the suppress: 2 red, the new test and test_an_interrupt_mid_write_leaves_only_the_destination, which reaches the same state incidentally because the discarded handle is collected before the cleanup runs. Restored, 75 pass. ruff and mypy clean.
